title: EIP-8442: 64-bit Opcodes for the EVM
description: Single-byte opcodes for 64-bit arithmetic, comparison, bitwise, and memory operations
author: Greg Colvin (@gcolvin) <greg@colvin.org>, Wei Tang (@sorpaas)
bodyPreview: ## Abstract Not every computation needs 256 bits. Counters, offsets, lengths, and the inner loops of hashes and big-number arithmetic fit in 64, and the EVM makes them pay for 256 at every step. This proposal adds twenty-eight instructions that compute on the low 64 bits of their operands: each is the *twin* of an existing arithmetic, comparison, bitwise, or memory instruction — the same operation at the same cost tier, one step down — at the existing opcode plus `0xC0`. The instructions take no immediate data and enter no mode: they mix freely with the rest of the instruction set, and every result is an ordinary 256-bit word. *Note: Significant assistance from AI is acknowledged, primarily for the reference implementation and its tests.* ## Motivation Most of the values a contract computes with fit in 64 bits. On the 64-bit machines that run the EVM a 256-bit addition is four limbs and three carries, a multiplication ten partial products, a comparison up to four; the same work on a 64-bit value is one instruction. An interpreter hides most of the difference behind its dispatch. Compiled code does not, and neither does a zero-knowledge (ZK) virtual machine, where the prover pays per RISC-V instruction executed. These instructions let code that fits in 64 bits pay for 64. Measured in [EIP-7979](./eip-7979.md)'s harness, they alone make a program 1.1x to 1.5x cheaper interpreted and 2.8x to 11x cheaper compiled. Together with validated static control flow they compound: compiled code executes 19x to 51x fewer RISC-V instructions than today's interpreted EVM, and a ZK prover's cost falls with it. The measurements are in the Rationale. ## Specification > *The key words MUST and MUST NOT in this Specification are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119 and RFC 8174.* The EVM's machine state includes a *data stack* of 256-bit words. These instructions leave it so. Each reads only the low 64 bits of its operands — the operand modulo 2^64 — and pushes a 64-bit result zero-extended to 256 bits: the high 192 bits of every result are zero. *Signed* instructions read the low 64 bits as a two's-complement integer. No mode is entered or left; the instructions may appear anywhere, in any mix with the rest of the instruction set. *Note: the zero high bits describe the result, not its storage. An implementation may keep a 64-bit value in one machine word and supply the zeros when a 256-bit instruction reads it.* ### The instructions Each instruction is the *twin* of an existing one — the same operation on 64-bit operands — at the existing opcode plus `0xC0`. In the table, *a* is the top of the *data stack*, *b* the item beneath it, and *N* the third, each read modulo 2^64; every result is reduced modulo 2^64; division truncates toward zero and division by zero yields zero. | Opcode | Instruction | Pops | Pushes | Cost | Result | |--------|-------------|-----:|-------:|------|--------| | `0xC1` | `ADD64` | 2 | 1 | *verylow64* | a + b | | `0xC2` | `MUL64` | 2 | 1 | *low64* | a × b | | `0xC3` | `SUB64` | 2 | 1 | *verylow64* | a - b | | `0xC4` | `DIV64` | 2 | 1 | *low64* | a / b | | `0xC5` | `SDIV64` | 2 | 1 | *low64* | a / b, signed | | `0xC6` | `MOD64` | 2 | 1 | *low64* | a mod b | | `0xC7` | `SMOD64` | 2 | 1 | *low64* | a mod b, signed, with the sign of a | | `0xC8` | `ADDMOD64` | 3 | 1 | *mid64* | (a + b) mod N, the sum not reduced; 0 if N = 0 | | `0xC9` | `MULMOD64` | 3 | 1 | *mid64* | (a × b) mod N, the product not reduced; 0 if N = 0 | | `0xCA` | `EXP64` | 2 | 1 | *exp64* | a to the power b | | `0xCB` | `SIGNEXTEND64` | 2 | 1 | *low64* | b sign-extended from bit 8a + 7; b if a > 6 | | `0xCC` | `CALLDATALOAD64` | 1 | 1 | *verylow64* | `CALLDATALOAD` of a, modulo 2^64 | | `0xCD` | `MLOAD64` | 1 | 1 | *verylow64* + memory | `MLOAD` of a, modulo 2^64 | | `0xCE` | `MSTORE64` | 2 | 0 | *verylow64* + memory | `MSTORE` of b modulo 2^64 at a | | `0xD0` | `LT64` | 2 | 1 | *verylow64* | 1 if a < b, else 0 | | `0xD1` | `GT64` | 2 | 1 | *verylow64* | 1 if a > b, else 0 | | `0xD2` | `SLT64` | 2 | 1 | *verylow64* | 1 if a < b, signed, else 0 | | `0xD3` | `SGT64` | 2 | 1 | *verylow64* | 1 if a > b, signed, else 0 | | `0xD4` | `EQ64` | 2 | 1 | *verylow64* | 1 if a = b, else 0 | | `0xD5` | `ISZERO64` | 1 | 1 | *verylow64* | 1 if a = 0, else 0 | | `0xD6` | `AND64` | 2 | 1 | *verylow64* | a and b, bitwise | | `0xD7` | `OR64` | 2 | 1 | *verylow64* | a or b, bitwise | | `0xD8` | `XOR64` | 2 | 1 | *verylow64* | a xor b, bitwise | | `0xD9` | `NOT64` | 1 | 1 | *verylow64* | not a, bitwise | | `0xDB` | `SHL64` | 2 | 1 | *verylow64* | b shifted left a bits; 0 if a > 63 | | `0xDC` | `SHR64` | 2 | 1 | *verylow64* | b shifted right a bits; 0 if a > 63 | | `0xDD` | `SAR64` | 2 | 1 | *verylow64* | b shifted right a bits, signed, filling with the sign of b | | `0xDE` | `CLZ64` | 1 | 1 | *low64* | the number of leading zero bits of a; 64 if a = 0 | `0xC0`, `0xCF`, `0xDA`, and `0xDF` are left unassigned. The three load and store instructions are their twins reduced modulo 2^64: the same 32-byte window at the same offset, the same memory expansion, the same bytes. `MLOAD64` reads the low eight bytes of the word `MLOAD` would read, so it reads back what `MSTORE` stored of a 64-bit value; `CALLDATALOAD64` reads the low eight bytes of a calldata word, so it reads an ABI-encoded 64-bit argument in place. `MSTORE64` writes the full 32-byte word, its high 24 bytes zero. ### Costs Four new tiers, each a step below the tier of the twin: *verylow64* is 2 where *verylow* is 3, *low64* is 3 where *low* is 5, *mid64* is 5 where *mid* is 8, and *exp64* is 5 plus 25 per byte of the exponent — the exponent being b modulo 2^64, so at most eight bytes — where `EXP` is 10 plus 50. `MLOAD64` and `MSTORE64` pay memory expansion exactly as `MLOAD` and `MSTORE` do. The discounts reflect the work: one machine word where the twin handles four, with no carries between limbs. Benchmarking will be needed to tell if the costs are well-balanced. ### Analysis Non
